50	
51	**Summary:** Completed Section 3 of the add-harnaas-foundation change — help groups, the explicit-attachment rule, the local --json flag helper and the stdout/stderr output contract — taking the change from 17/74 to 22/74 tasks with fmt, lint and tests all clean.
52	
53	**Changes:**
54	- cmd/harnaas/cli/root.go declares the root's help groups (setup, then assets) in display order, and adds addCommand(parent, child, groupID) as the single way a command joins the tree: it declares the group on first use, sets the child's GroupID, and panics naming command and group on an unknown id — surfacing a wiring typo at construction instead of cobra's execute-time panic

57	- cmd/harnaas/cli/output.go states the output contract in one place and implements it: printJSON writes the document to cmd.OutOrStdout() indented, with HTML escaping off so an ampersand in a source ref survives verbatim, and newline-terminated; advisef sends progress and warning text to cmd.ErrOrStderr()
58	- cmd/harnaas/cli/root_test.go covers section 3.5 and 3.2: the root declares no persistent flags and a subcommand inherits nothing; --json is accepted only on the command that declares it and fails as 'unknown flag: --json' on a sibling and on the root; groups are declared in display order and none is declared empty; addCommand rejects an unknown group; and an AST pass over non-test sources asserts the package declares no init, so the no-self-registration rule survives a gochecknoinits suppression
59	- cmd/harnaas/cli/output_test.go proves stdout carries a single parseable JSON document while advisef output lands on stderr, that the ampersand is not rewritten to its HTML escape, that the document ends in exactly one newline, and that an unencodable value returns an error rather than truncating stdout

63	- Cobra renders a help header for every declared group whether or not it has members — verified with a scratch test showing a bare 'Empty Commands:' line. That is why helpGroups is a declaration list and addCommand declares a group only on first use: eager declaration would show empty headings for install and lint until their own changes land. The cost is that group display order equals command attachment order, which TestHelpGroupsAreDeclaredInDisplayOrder pins.
64	- Cobra's checkCommandGroups panics at execute time for a command whose GroupID names an undeclared group, but AddCommand itself does no checking — so a group declared after the commands that use it is a latent panic, not a compile error.
65	- Section 3.5's 'wrong positional-argument count prints the subcommand's usage' and 'an unrecognized subcommand exits non-zero' were already covered by iteration 2's main_test.go (TestReportErrorShowsTheDeepestSubcommandUsageForAnArgCountError and TestErrorSwitchClassifiesRealCobraErrors); only the persistent-flag and unknown---json assertions were still missing.

67	- golangci-lint's `unused` counts usage from _test.go files, so addJSONFlag, jsonRequested, printJSON, advisef and addCommand stay lint-clean while no command uses them yet.

69	- Asserting 'the HTML escape is absent' needs the escape written as a Go interpreted string ("\\u0026"), not a raw-string literal — a raw string containing the bare character makes the assertion trivially fail against its own input.

71	### Iteration 4
72	
73	**Summary:** Added the paths and logging foundation packages (tasks 4.2 and 4.3) and wired both into the entrypoint, taking the add-harnaas-foundation change from 22/74 to 24/74 tasks with fmt, lint and tests all clean.
74	
75	**Changes:**
76	- cmd/harnaas/cli/paths resolves the project root by walking up for a .git marker — accepting the file form git writes in a worktree or submodule, and letting the nearest enclosing repository win as git itself does — through a pure Resolve(startDir) that takes a directory rather than reading one
77	- paths.WithDiscoveredRoot is the single sanctioned reader of the process working directory, carrying the resolved root or the failure in the context; the forbidigo suppression lives there, inside the abstraction the ban's message names
78	- paths.ProjectRoot(ctx) surfaces the discovery failure at the moment a command asks for a root, so --version, --help and an unknown-command diagnostic keep working outside a repository; a context that never established a root reports ErrRootNotEstablished as a wiring failure distinct from the user-facing *NoProjectRootError
79	- *NoProjectRootError is typed so a command can recognise the condition without matching message text, and renders as problem-then-fix: which directory was searched, then to run harnaas inside a repository or create one with git init
80	- cmd/harnaas/cli/logging writes structured slog records to a file under the user's cache directory (HARNAAS_LOG_FILE overrides it, HARNAAS_LOG_LEVEL sets the threshold, both documented at their only read site), never to a terminal stream
81	- logging discards records where the log file cannot be opened, rather than the reference CLI's fallback to stderr, and Open returns no error because there is nowhere to report one to — a warning on the terminal is the interleaving the log file exists to prevent
82	- logging.WithCommand and logging.WithComponent label every record with the command the user ran and the subsystem that produced it, ahead of the call site's own attributes; the API takes slog.Attr only, so every logged value arrives as a named field
83	- The package doc states the privacy rule as a hard rule with harnaas's own reason: the files it handles are a team's instructions and rules, exactly the content nobody expects to find copied into a log they did not know existed
84	- main.go establishes the project root and opens the log before executing the command tree, and records the run's outcome by exit code and error *type* — never the error message, because errors from later phases will quote the manifest that produced them
85	- Test coverage: resolution from a nested directory matching resolution from the root, the marker-file form, the nearest-repository rule, the outside-a-repository diagnostic naming directory and fix, context carrying and key isolation, plus logging tests that redirect stdout, stderr and slog's default logger and assert on cleanup that nothing reached any of them
86	- CLAUDE.md's logging section now records the two load-bearing decisions — discard rather than fall back to a stream, and keep the log outside the project — so a later change does not reintroduce either
87	
88	**Learnings:**
89	- Logging cannot live under the project: task 8.11 requires that after init no .harnaas/ directory exists and harnaas.json is the only file that appeared, so the log file must go under os.UserCacheDir. Task 9.5's 'redirect home, cache and config under t.TempDir' harness confirms per-user state is where harnaas keeps everything that is not the manifest.
90	- The reference CLI's logging falls back to stderr when the log file cannot be opened; copying that would corrupt a --json document, so harnaas discards instead. The uninitialised logger must also be a discarding logger rather than slog.Default(), which writes to stderr — a stray log call before Open would otherwise print.
91	- sloglint's attr-only: true is already configured in .golangci.yaml, which is the mechanical half of task 4.3's 'attribute-only API'; taking ...slog.Attr in the wrapper signatures makes it a compile-time guarantee at harnaas's own call sites too.
92	- staticcheck ST1005 rejects an errors.New string ending in punctuation or a newline, which rules out the problem-blank-line-fix diagnostic shape for a sentinel error. Giving the sentinel a small unexported type with an Error() method keeps errors.Is working and keeps the message shaped like every other diagnostic.
93	- sloglint also rejects slog.NewJSONHandler(io.Discard, ...) in favour of Go 1.24's slog.DiscardHandler, and gocritic's mapKey flags a table-test map key with leading or trailing whitespace — a case worth testing, so that table has to be a slice of structs.
94	- t.Chdir forbids t.Parallel, which is the practical argument for making root resolution a pure function over a directory: only the one test that exercises WithDiscoveredRoot has to move the process, and every other paths test runs in parallel.
95	- t.TempDir sits under a symlink on macOS (/var → /private/var), so a root discovered through the working directory comes back spelled differently from the path the test created; the paths tests resolve symlinks in their scratch-directory helper rather than teaching the package to rewrite paths.
96	- errcheck's check-blank: true makes `_ = f()` on an error a lint failure, so a deliberately-ignored error needs a real branch or a signature that returns no error at all — which pushed logging.Open to return only its closer, with the unexported open(path) keeping the failure visible to tests.
97	
98	### Iteration 5
99	
100	**Summary:** Added the palette and jsonutil foundation packages (tasks 4.4 and 4.6) and routed the --json output path through jsonutil's canonical encoder, taking the add-harnaas-foundation change from 24/74 to 26/74 tasks with fmt, lint and tests all clean.
101	
102	**Changes:**
103	- cmd/harnaas/cli/palette is a zero-dependency package of base16 ANSI slot constants held as plain strings, so harnaas's colours are a request the terminal answers with the user's own theme rather than a hex value that is only correct on the machine it was picked on
104	- palette's semantic aliases (Accent, Accent2, Muted, Success, Error, Warning, Info) are what styles declare against, with the raw slot names reserved for colour that carries no meaning; the package documents that one Muted slot rather than a range of greys is what keeps de-emphasis reading as one level
105	- palette deliberately declares no body-text alias, and the package comment states why: body text stays unstyled so it renders in the terminal's default foreground and inverts with the background, where pinning White would erase every line on a light terminal
106	- palette's tests read the package's own source via AST so a colour added later is covered without anyone remembering to extend the test, assert every declared colour is a slot in 0..15, assert no alias name reads as body text, and assert no two semantic aliases collapse onto the same slot
107	- cmd/harnaas/cli/jsonutil.Marshal is harnaas's single JSON document format — two-space indent, HTML left unescaped so an ampersand in a source ref survives, and exactly one trailing newline — with the indent a constant rather than a parameter because the whole point is that a manifest and a --json document are not formatted differently for want of a shared default
108	- jsonutil.WriteFileAtomic stages the bytes in a sibling file in the destination directory, flushes them to disk, applies the permission and renames over the destination, so a reader sees either the whole old file or the whole new one; staging beside the destination is what keeps the rename a rename rather than a cross-filesystem copy
109	- WriteFileAtomic removes the staging file unconditionally via defer on both success and failure, and flushes the destination directory best-effort after the rename so a crash cannot leave new contents on disk behind a directory entry still pointing at the old file
110	- WriteFileAtomic delegates to an unexported writeFileAtomic taking the flush step as a parameter, giving the failure-path guarantee a test seam without a mutable global, so the injected-failure tests still run in parallel
111	- jsonutil tests cover the format line by line (indentation is what is under test), HTML characters left verbatim, the single trailing newline, a round trip, an unencodable value returning no partial document, file creation and full replacement of a longer previous file, permission application, an unusable destination directory, and the two injected-failure cases — previous file intact and nothing created — each asserting on the directory's entries so no staging file can survive under a name the test would have to guess
112	- printJSON in cmd/harnaas/cli/output.go now encodes through jsonutil.Marshal and writes the finished bytes, so the --json document and the manifest init will write share one definition of the format, and an unencodable value returns an error with stdout still empty instead of a half-streamed document ahead of the entrypoint's error message
113	- Tasks 4.4 and 4.6 checked off in openspec/changes/add-harnaas-foundation/tasks.md; 4.7 left unchecked because its accessible-mode and piped-stream clauses depend on 4.5's uiform and interactive packages
114	
115	**Learnings:**
116	- golangci-lint's std-error-handling exclusion preset already covers os.Remove and *.Close, so `_ = os.Remove(...)` and a deferred Close stay clean even with errcheck's check-blank: true — but Sync is not on that list, so the best-effort directory flush still needs an explicit nolint with a reason. This is the boundary that decides which dropped errors need a suppression and which do not.
117	- testifylint's encoded-compare rule rejects asserting an exact JSON string with assert.Equal and pushes toward assert.JSONEq, which would defeat a test whose whole subject is indentation and trailing newline. Splitting the document on newlines and comparing the resulting []string satisfies the linter and reads better, because a failure names the line that moved.
118	- Injecting a mid-write failure portably needs a seam: making the rename fail is platform-specific (POSIX rename over a regular file succeeds), so passing the flush step as a function parameter to an unexported implementation is the way to exercise the failure path on both Windows and POSIX. Unlike a package-level var it does not force the test to give up t.Parallel.
119	- On Windows the staging file must be closed before the deferred os.Remove can delete it, so the write/flush/close sequence has to close on every path including the ones where write or flush failed — otherwise the 'no staging file survives' guarantee holds on POSIX and silently fails on Windows.
120	- os.Chmod on Windows only toggles a read-only bit rather than storing the requested mode, so the permission assertion has to skip there; the file-contents and no-litter assertions still run on every platform.
121	- The `check` mise task fans out fmt, lint:go, lint:gofmt, lint:gomod, lint:mise and lint:shellcheck but not lint:licenses — that gate is a separate task, so a change adding dependencies has to run it explicitly.
122	
123	### Iteration 6
124	
125	**Summary:** Added the interactive and uiform foundation packages (tasks 4.5 and 4.7), completing Section 4 of the add-harnaas-foundation change and taking it from 26/74 to 28/74 tasks with fmt, lint and tests all clean.
126	
127	**Changes:**
128	- cmd/harnaas/cli/interactive resolves whether harnaas may prompt from the command's own streams plus the environment — HARNAAS_TEST_TTY override, then go test, then coding-agent sentinels (CLAUDECODE, CURSOR_AGENT, GEMINI_CLI, COPILOT_CLI, PI_CODING_AGENT), then CI, then both streams being terminals — with the decision biased towards 'no' because a flag-driven path always exists while a prompt shown to something that cannot answer hangs rather than degrades
129	- interactive deliberately tests the attached streams rather than probing a controlling terminal, which keeps the question answerable on Windows and keeps it honest under redirection: `harnaas init > out.txt` has a terminal attached to the process and still must not prompt
130	- interactive.ShouldStyle is the single gate in front of the palette, honouring NO_COLOR and excluding TERM=cygwin, and is kept a separate question from CanPrompt because a run inside a coding agent must not be prompted and may still be styled
131	- Both decisions are split into pure cores (canPrompt, shouldStyle) taking getenv and the terminal answer as parameters, because `go test` can never present a real terminal and the exported functions would short-circuit before the environment gates were reached
132	- cmd/harnaas/cli/uiform is the only place harnaas builds a form, so accessible mode and the base16 theme are applied without anyone having to remember them; New takes explicit streams so prompts render on stderr and cannot corrupt a --json document on stdout
133	- uiform.Theme unsets the pinned foreground on titles and unselected options in both the focused and blurred variants so they inherit the terminal's default text colour, and points selection at palette.Accent — the theme declares no colour of its own
134	- uiform.Confirm returns ErrCancelled for a dismissed prompt rather than folding cancellation into a 'no', because the init spec requires a cancelled prompt to write nothing and exit non-zero while a decline is an ordinary answer
135	- uiform.Confirm consults the context directly before and after running the form, because huh reports a cancelled context as ErrTimeout and ignores the context entirely in accessible mode
136	- Test coverage: a table over every prompting gate including piped streams and the CI=false escape hatch, each agent sentinel individually, real os.Pipe and bytes.Buffer both answering 'not a terminal', the styling gates, accessible mode completing a prompt against non-terminal streams, cancellation reported separately from declining, and the theme's unstyled-titles and accent-selection guarantees
137	- charm.land/huh/v2, charm.land/lipgloss/v2 and golang.org/x/term added to go.mod, with the go-licenses gate confirming all 20 new transitive dependencies are on the allowlist
138	- CLAUDE.md's non-interactive completeness section now records the two load-bearing decisions — prompting resolved from streams rather than a controlling terminal, and a cancelled prompt distinct from a 'no' — so a later change does not reintroduce either
139	- Tasks 4.5 and 4.7 checked off in openspec/changes/add-harnaas-foundation/tasks.md, completing Section 4
140	
141	**Learnings:**
142	- huh v2 reports a cancelled context as huh.ErrTimeout, not ErrUserAborted or context.Canceled — its run() maps tea.ErrProgramKilled to ErrTimeout because a timeout is the only reason it cancels a context itself. Matching on huh's error alone silently misclassifies a signal-driven cancellation; consulting ctx.Err() is the only reliable test.
143	- huh's accessible path (runAccessible) ignores the context entirely and runs synchronously against the given reader/writer, so a cancellation arriving mid-question is invisible until the prompt returns. Any wrapper that must honour cancellation has to check the context after the run as well as before it.
144	- Accessible mode is what makes a prompt testable at all: the full-screen path needs a terminal to redraw, while runAccessible works against a strings.Reader and a bytes.Buffer. A test that sets ACCESSIBLE and completes a prompt on non-terminal streams is therefore a genuine assertion that accessible mode was honoured, not a proxy for one.
145	- huh's accessible PromptString breaks out of its re-prompt loop on EOF rather than looping forever, and an empty line falls through to the default — so a test can feed a bare reader without hanging.
146	- The reference CLI's /dev/tty probe plus raw-mode ioctl is POSIX-only and would need three build-tagged files that do nothing on Windows. Testing the command's own streams for terminal-ness covers the same cases portably and additionally catches redirection, which the /dev/tty probe misses.
147	- lint:gomod necessarily fails in any iteration that adds a dependency, because it runs `go mod tidy` and then asserts `git status --porcelain go.mod go.sum` is empty — uncommitted additions are indistinguishable from an untidy tree. The signal to check is that `go mod tidy` produced no *further* change beyond the intended one.
148	- golangci-lint accepted the whole huh/lipgloss surface without a single suppression beyond the two gosec G115 fd conversions, so the charm v2 stack imposes no lint debt on this configuration.
149	
150	### Iteration 7
151	
152	**Summary:** Added the data-only harness roster package (Section 5, tasks 5.1–5.4), taking the add-harnaas-foundation change from 28/74 to 32/74 tasks with fmt, lint and tests all clean.
153	
154	**Changes:**
155	- cmd/harnaas/cli/harness declares the Harness descriptor — canonical ID (a named string type so a source key or display name cannot be passed as a harness), display name, PerUserLocation, and ProjectEvidence — with claude-code as the only roster entry and Default pointing at it
156	- Project evidence is held as project-root-relative paths ('.claude', 'CLAUDE.md') rather than a predicate, so init does the stat calls and the roster holds no behaviour the install adapters could later disagree with
157	- Lookup helpers: IDs() and All() returning deep copies in the roster's sorted order, Lookup, Recognized, and HasPerUserLocation as the query manifest scope validation calls
158	- *UnknownError carries the id exactly as written plus the recognized list, and renders problem-then-fix so a caller can attribute the failure to an asset entry without matching message text; HasPerUserLocation returns that error for an unknown id rather than false, because a typo and an unsupported scope need different edits
159	- Tests cover the default being itself recognized, sorted and call-stable ordering, the unknown-id message naming the input and listing alternatives identically on every run, every entry being usable with relative non-escaping evidence, and callers being unable to mutate the roster through All() or IDs()
160	- Two AST guardrails over non-test sources: the package imports no filesystem, network or environment package (encoding 'data only, no write behaviour'), and declares no package init so the roster stays a readable literal
161	- CLAUDE.md records the two load-bearing decisions — the roster is data only with the caller doing I/O, and an unrecognized id is an error because the harnesses list states a guarantee rather than exclusivity
162	- Tasks 5.1 through 5.4 checked off in openspec/changes/add-harnaas-foundation/tasks.md

Implement tasks from an OpenSpec change.

**Store selection:** If the user names a store (a store is a standalone OpenSpec repo registered on this machine) or the work lives in one, run `openspec store list --json` to discover registered store ids, then pass `--store <id>` on the commands that read or write specs and changes (`new change`, `status`, `instructions`, `list`, `show`, `validate`, `archive`, `doctor`, `context`, `view`). Once selected, treat `--store <id>` as sticky for the rest of the workflow. Every unscoped example of those commands below is shorthand: before running it, append the flag. For example, run `openspec status --change "<name>" --json --store "<id>"`, not the unscoped form shown below. Other commands do not take the flag. Hints printed by commands already carry the flag; keep it on follow-ups. Without a store, commands act on the nearest local `openspec/` root.

**Input**: Optionally specify a change name (e.g., `/opsx:apply add-auth`). If omitted, check if it can be inferred from conversation context. If vague or ambiguous you MUST prompt for available changes.

**Steps**

1. **Select the change**

   If a name is provided, use it. Otherwise:
   - Infer from conversation context if the user mentioned a change
   - Auto-select if only one active change exists
   - If ambiguous, run `openspec list --json` to get available changes and ask the user to select one

   Always announce: "Using change: <name>" and how to override (e.g., `/opsx:apply <other>`).

2. **Check status to understand the schema**
   ```bash
   openspec status --change "<name>" --json
   ```
   Parse the JSON to understand:
   - `schemaName`: The workflow being used (e.g., "spec-driven")
   - `planningHome`, `changeRoot`, and `actionContext`: planning scope and edit constraints
   - Which artifact contains the tasks (typically "tasks" for spec-driven, check status for others)

3. **Get apply instructions**

   ```bash
   openspec instructions apply --change "<name>" --json
   ```

   This returns:
   - `contextFiles`: artifact ID -> array of concrete file paths (varies by schema - could be proposal/specs/design/tasks or spec/tests/implementation/docs)
   - Progress (total, complete, remaining)
   - Task list with status
   - Dynamic instruction based on current state
   - Optional `context`: current required project instruction input from the selected root
   - Optional `operationGuidance`: current advisory guidance for apply

   **Handle states:**
   - If `state: "blocked"` (missing artifacts): show message, suggest using `/opsx:continue` (if it is not installed, run `openspec status --change "<name>" --json` to see the next artifact and `openspec instructions <artifact-id> --change "<name>" --json` for how to create it)
   - If `state: "all_done"`: congratulate, suggest archive
   - Otherwise: proceed to implementation

   Treat `context` as a required prompt-level input. Read and consider it, and
   apply relevant project facts, conventions, and constraints while implementing.
   Treat `operationGuidance` as optional additive advice. Read and consider every
   entry, and follow entries that are applicable and compatible with the built-in
   workflow.

   Keep both fields separate from CLI-returned state, missing artifacts, tasks,
   progress, `contextFiles`, and the built-in `instruction`. They are not
   evidence of task completion, do not replace the built-in instruction, and do
   not permit bypassing a blocked state. If context conflicts with the built-in
   instruction, an explicit user choice, or a CLI-controlled value, report the
   conflict and preserve the controlling value. If guidance is inapplicable or
   conflicts with those controlling inputs, do not follow it and explain why.
   These are prompt-level behavior contracts, not enforceable checks.

4. **Read context files**

   Read every file path listed under `contextFiles` from the apply instructions output.
   The files depend on the schema being used:
   - **spec-driven**: proposal, specs, design, tasks
   - Other schemas: follow the contextFiles from CLI output

   Do not copy `context` or `operationGuidance` verbatim into implementation
   files or planning artifacts unless the user separately asks for that content.

5. **Show current progress**

   Display:
   - Schema being used
   - Progress: "N/M tasks complete"
   - Remaining tasks overview
   - Dynamic instruction from CLI

6. **Implement tasks (loop until done or blocked)**

   For each pending task:
   - Show which task is being worked on
   - Make the code changes required
   - Keep changes minimal and focused
   - Mark task complete in the tasks file: `- [ ]` → `- [x]`
   - Continue to next task

   **Pause if:**
   - Task is unclear → ask for clarification
   - Implementation reveals a design issue → suggest updating artifacts
   - Error or blocker encountered → report and wait for guidance
   - User interrupts

7. **On completion or pause, show status**

   Display:
   - Tasks completed this session
   - Overall progress: "N/M tasks complete"
   - If all done: suggest archive
   - If paused: explain why and wait for guidance

**Output During Implementation**

```
## Implementing: <change-name> (schema: <schema-name>)

Working on task 3/7: <task description>
[...implementation happening...]
✓ Task complete

Working on task 4/7: <task description>
[...implementation happening...]
✓ Task complete
```

**Output On Completion**

```
## Implementation Complete

**Change:** <change-name>
**Schema:** <schema-name>
**Progress:** 7/7 tasks complete ✓

### Completed This Session
- [x] Task 1
- [x] Task 2
...

All tasks complete! You can archive this change with `/opsx:archive`.
```

**Output On Pause (Issue Encountered)**

```
## Implementation Paused

**Change:** <change-name>
**Schema:** <schema-name>
**Progress:** 4/7 tasks complete

### Issue Encountered
<description of the issue>

**Options:**
1. <option 1>
2. <option 2>
3. Other approach

What would you like to do?
```

**Guardrails**
- Keep going through tasks until done or blocked
- Always read context files before starting (from the apply instructions output)
- If task is ambiguous, pause and ask before implementing
- If implementation reveals issues, pause and suggest artifact updates
- Keep code changes minimal and scoped to each task
- Update task checkbox immediately after completing each task
- Pause on errors, blockers, or unclear requirements - don't guess
- Use contextFiles from CLI output, don't assume specific file names
- Do not use context or operation guidance as proof that a task is complete
- Apply relevant project context; report conflicts with controlling workflow inputs
- Consider every guidance entry; explain any inapplicable or conflicting advice
- Do not copy runtime context or operation guidance into implementation files or planning artifacts
- Preserve CLI-controlled blocked/ready/all-done behavior and completion criteria

**Fluid Workflow Integration**

This skill supports the "actions on a change" model:

- **Can be invoked anytime**: Before all artifacts are done (if tasks exist), after partial implementation, interleaved with other actions
- **Allows artifact updates**: If implementation reveals design issues, suggest updating artifacts - not phase-locked, work fluidly

1	## Purpose
2	
3	Defines how a declared asset source becomes a verified set of files on disk: resolving a GitHub ref
4	to an immutable commit, retrieving and extracting the repository archive, reading local sources under
5	the project's `.harnaas` directory, verifying that what arrived has the shape its asset type
6	requires, and computing the content digests that install and lint both depend on. It also fixes the
7	transport security, caching, authentication and offline rules for every fetch the CLI makes.
8	
9	## ADDED Requirements
10	
11	### Requirement: Source Kind Registry
12	
13	Source kinds SHALL be resolved through a registry keyed by kind name, so a new kind can be added
14	without modifying the install flow. Every kind SHALL expose the same contract: given a normalized
15	source, produce a resolved set of files plus the provenance facts needed to record and later re-check
16	it. Version 1 SHALL register the kinds `github` and `local`.
17	
18	#### Scenario: Registered kind resolves through the common contract
19	
20	- **WHEN** an asset declares a source of a registered kind
21	- **THEN** the install flow resolves it through the registry without kind-specific branching
22	
23	#### Scenario: Unregistered kind fails before any side effect
24	
25	- **WHEN** a source names a kind that is not registered
26	- **THEN** resolution fails naming the unsupported kind, and no network request or filesystem write
27	  occurs
28	
29	### Requirement: GitHub Ref Resolution
30	
31	A `github` source SHALL be resolved to an immutable commit identifier over the Git protocol, reusing
32	the ambient Git credential helpers, before any content is fetched. A tag or branch ref SHALL be
33	resolved against the remote repository; a ref that is already a full commit identifier SHALL be used
34	directly; an absent ref SHALL resolve the repository's default branch. The resolved commit SHALL be
35	reported alongside the content so it can be recorded.
36	
37	#### Scenario: Tag resolves to a commit
38	
39	- **WHEN** a source declares the ref `v1.2.0`
40	- **THEN** resolution produces the commit that tag points at, and that commit is what content is
41	  fetched from
42	
43	#### Scenario: Branch resolves to its current tip
44	
45	- **WHEN** a source declares a branch ref
46	- **THEN** resolution produces the branch's current tip commit and reports the ref as mutable
47	
48	#### Scenario: Commit identifier is used directly
49	
50	- **WHEN** a source declares a full commit identifier as its ref
51	- **THEN** no remote ref lookup is required and that commit is used
52	
53	#### Scenario: Unknown ref is reported clearly
54	
55	- **WHEN** a source declares a ref that does not exist in the remote repository
56	- **THEN** resolution fails naming the asset, the repository, and the missing ref
57	
58	### Requirement: Repository Archive Retrieval
59	
60	Content for a `github` source SHALL be obtained by fetching the repository archive for the resolved
61	commit over HTTPS, rather than by requesting files individually, and SHALL be fetched at most once
62	per repository and commit per run. A retrieval failure SHALL name the asset, the repository and the
63	resolved commit, and MUST NOT be treated as the source resolving to empty content.
64	
65	#### Scenario: Multiple assets from one repository share a fetch
66	
67	- **WHEN** several assets reference different paths within the same repository at the same resolved
68	  commit
69	- **THEN** the archive is fetched once and every asset is extracted from it
70	
71	#### Scenario: Fetch failure names the asset
72	
73	- **WHEN** the archive cannot be retrieved
74	- **THEN** resolution fails identifying the asset, the repository and the resolved commit
75	
76	#### Scenario: Network failure never yields empty content
77	
78	- **WHEN** the remote host is unreachable
79	- **THEN** resolution fails naming the asset and the host, and no asset is treated as resolving to
80	  empty content
81	
82	### Requirement: Transport Security
83	
84	Every network fetch SHALL use HTTPS and MUST reject a plaintext or loopback destination, including
85	one reached by redirect. Redirects SHALL be followed only up to a bounded limit. Response bodies
86	SHALL be read under a size ceiling and MUST fail rather than truncate when the ceiling is exceeded.
87	Credentials MUST NOT be written to disk or included in any error message.
88	
89	#### Scenario: Plaintext destination is refused
90	
91	- **WHEN** a fetch would be made over a non-HTTPS scheme
92	- **THEN** the request is refused before it is sent and resolution fails reporting the insecure
93	  destination
94	
95	#### Scenario: Redirect to an insecure destination is refused
96	
97	- **WHEN** an HTTPS request redirects to a plaintext or loopback destination
98	- **THEN** the redirect is not followed and resolution fails
99	
100	#### Scenario: Redirect chain is bounded
101	
102	- **WHEN** a request exceeds the redirect limit
103	- **THEN** the fetch fails reporting too many redirects rather than following indefinitely
104	
105	#### Scenario: Oversized response fails rather than truncates
106	
107	- **WHEN** a response body exceeds the configured size ceiling
108	- **THEN** the fetch fails reporting the limit, and no partial content is used
109	
110	#### Scenario: Credentials are redacted from errors
111	
112	- **WHEN** a fetch fails against a URL that carried credentials
113	- **THEN** the reported error contains the destination with its credentials removed
114	
115	### Requirement: Archive Extraction Safety
116	
117	Extraction SHALL take only the subtree named by the source's path and SHALL reject any archive entry
118	whose destination would fall outside the extraction root, including entries using absolute paths or
119	upward traversal. Symbolic-link, hard-link and device entries MUST be rejected rather than
120	materialized. Individual entry sizes and the total extracted size SHALL be bounded.
121	
122	#### Scenario: Only the declared subtree is extracted
123	
124	- **WHEN** a source names a path within a repository
125	- **THEN** only files under that path are extracted, and the extracted paths are relative to it
126	
127	#### Scenario: Traversing entry is rejected
128	
129	- **WHEN** an archive contains an entry whose path escapes the extraction root
130	- **THEN** extraction fails reporting the offending entry and nothing is written outside the root
131	
132	#### Scenario: Link entry is rejected
133	
134	- **WHEN** an archive contains a symbolic-link or hard-link entry within the selected subtree
135	- **THEN** extraction fails reporting that links are not supported in harness assets
136	
137	#### Scenario: Extraction size ceiling is enforced
138	
139	- **WHEN** the selected subtree exceeds the total extraction size ceiling
140	- **THEN** extraction fails reporting the limit and no partially extracted content is used
141	
142	#### Scenario: Missing path in repository is reported
143	
144	- **WHEN** the source's path does not exist at the resolved commit
145	- **THEN** resolution fails naming the asset, the path and the commit
146	
147	### Requirement: Local Source Reading
148	
149	A `local` source SHALL be read from the project's `.harnaas` directory through a confined handle
150	anchored at that directory, so no read can escape it even via a symbolic link created after
151	validation. A source that does not exist SHALL fail naming the expected path relative to the project
152	root.
153	
154	#### Scenario: Local file is read
155	
156	- **WHEN** an asset declares a local source that exists under `.harnaas`
157	- **THEN** its content is read and made available for installation
158	
159	#### Scenario: Symlink escaping .harnaas is refused
160	
161	- **WHEN** a path under `.harnaas` is a symbolic link pointing outside that directory
162	- **THEN** the read is refused and resolution fails reporting the containment violation
163	
164	#### Scenario: Missing local source is reported
165	
166	- **WHEN** a local source names a path that does not exist
167	- **THEN** resolution fails naming the asset and the expected path relative to the project root
168	
169	### Requirement: Source Shape Verification
170	
171	A resolved source SHALL be verified against the shape its asset type requires before installation is
172	planned. A `skill` source MUST resolve to a directory containing `SKILL.md`. A `rule`, `instruction`,
173	`command` or `persona` source MUST resolve to a single regular file. A mismatch SHALL be reported
174	naming the asset, its type, the expected shape and what was found instead.
175	
176	#### Scenario: Skill source must be a directory
177	
178	- **WHEN** an asset of type `skill` resolves to a single file
179	- **THEN** resolution fails reporting that a skill source must be a directory
180	
181	#### Scenario: Skill without SKILL.md is rejected
182	
183	- **WHEN** an asset of type `skill` resolves to a directory containing no `SKILL.md`
184	- **THEN** resolution fails naming the asset and the missing `SKILL.md`
185	
186	#### Scenario: Single-file type resolving to a directory is rejected
187	
188	- **WHEN** an asset of type `persona` resolves to a directory
189	- **THEN** resolution fails reporting that this asset type requires a single file
190	
191	#### Scenario: Every non-skill type is held to the single-file shape
192

1	## Context
2	
3	This change turns the declaration fixed in `add-harnaas-foundation` into filesystem effects. Four
4	things make it harder than "download and copy".
5	
6	- **The destinations are directories the user already owns.** `.agents/skills/` holds both assets a
7	  team declared and a skill somebody wrote yesterday, and nothing on disk distinguishes them. Getting
8	  ownership wrong means either clobbering work or never being able to update anything.
9	- **The same content has to be re-identified later.** `lint` must answer "did somebody edit this?"
10	  and "has upstream moved?" independently, and both are only answerable from what install recorded at
11	  the time it ran.
12	- **Harnesses fail silently.** A skill whose frontmatter `name` disagrees with its directory is
13	  dropped without a message on at least three harnesses; a memory file over 4 MiB is skipped; a write
14	  to a surface a harness removed is a no-op that looks exactly like success. A tool that installs into
15	  those conditions reports a lie.
16	- **This is the first network access, the first write outside the project's own files and the first
17	  archive extraction in the CLI**, so the security rules set here are the ones every later feature
18	  inherits.
19	
20	A survey of 23 harnesses reshaped the change: 17 read `.agents/skills/<id>/SKILL.md` and 21 read
21	`AGENTS.md`, so the obvious architecture — one adapter per supported harness — is not what this
22	builds. Most harnesses are served with no adapter at all, and an adapter is needed only for the
23	surfaces that have no shared equivalent. See
24	[0002-shared-agents-target-before-per-harness.md](../../../docs/adr/0002-shared-agents-target-before-per-harness.md).
25	
26	The entire.io CLI's managed-plugin subsystem solves the analogous problem for binaries and supplies
27	most of the mechanics — tag resolution over Git, download over HTTPS, archive entry safety, atomic
28	staging. The decisions below are where harness assets differ from executables.
29	
30	## Goals / Non-Goals
31	
32	**Goals**
33	
34	- Never destroy work the user did not delegate to `harnaas`.
35	- Never produce a silent no-op. Every condition a harness would ignore without saying so is turned
36	  into a visible refusal or a named outcome.
37	- Make an install reproducible: the same manifest and lockfile on another machine produce the same
38	  files.
39	- Record enough provenance that `lint` needs no bookkeeping of its own.
40	- Serve the many harnesses that read shared locations without writing an adapter for each, while
41	  keeping harness-specific knowledge behind one boundary so a second adapter is purely additive.
42	
43	**Non-Goals**
44	
45	- Signature or attestation verification. Digests here establish *integrity over time*, not
46	  *authenticity of origin*; a trust model needs a key-distribution story that does not exist yet.
47	- Transitive dependencies between assets. Every asset resolves independently.
48	- Interactive conflict resolution or merging. Conflicts are reported with a remedy; the user decides.
49	- Forges other than GitHub, and adapters other than `claude-code`. The two registries exist so that
50	  adding either does not reshape the flow.
51	- Implementing the format-converting renderers. They are named by the contract in v1 and deliberately
52	  left unbuilt.
53	- An `uninstall` command. Emptying the manifest's `assets` array and installing does it, and keeps
54	  convergence as the single code path that removes anything.
55	
56	## Decisions
57	
58	### Shared targets first; a named adapter is the exception
59	
60	Recorded in
61	[0002-shared-agents-target-before-per-harness.md](../../../docs/adr/0002-shared-agents-target-before-per-harness.md).
62	Its consequence for this change is structural: support is two-tiered. `skill` and `instruction` reach
63	a harness through shared locations with no per-harness code, while `rule`, `command` and `persona` —
64	which have no shared equivalent anywhere — reach it only through a named adapter. v1 ships exactly one
65	named adapter and still serves most of the ecosystem, and "harness with no adapter" is a supported
66	state rather than a gap.
67	
68	This is also why the `harnesses` list in the manifest means "the harnesses we guarantee", not "the
69	harnesses that will see this". A shared directory is visible to every harness installed on the
70	machine. Nothing in the design can change that, so the lockfile records which harness an adapter
71	resolved a destination *for*, as attribution rather than exclusive ownership.
72	
73	### Ownership lives in the lockfile
74	
75	Recorded in
76	[0001-ownership-lives-in-the-lockfile.md](../../../docs/adr/0001-ownership-lives-in-the-lockfile.md).
77	Two consequences are specified rather than left implicit, because both look like bugs if you meet
78	them without the rule: deleting the lockfile does not orphan installed files, it makes them
79	unmanaged, which is protective; and a project with pre-existing harness files gets conflict reports on
80	its first install rather than a silent takeover.
81	
82	The shared-target decision sharpens this. Ownership in `.agents/` is a seventeen-way problem, and
83	other tools write there too. The lockfile rule is what makes that safe without negotiation: another
84	tool's file at a destination `harnaas` wants is simply an unmanaged conflict — reported, never
85	overwritten.
86	
87	### Force applies to drift, never to unmanaged files
88	
89	`--force` overwrites a managed destination whose content no longer matches what was recorded. It
90	deliberately does not override unmanaged-path protection. The two situations look similar and are
91	not. A drifted managed file is something `harnaas` put there and the user edited, so restoring it is
92	recoverable and comprehensible. An unmanaged file was never `harnaas`'s, and no flag on an install
93	command should be able to destroy it. A user who wants `harnaas` to own that path deletes it
94	themselves, which is an explicit act with an obvious meaning.
95	
96	### Rendering is the general case; verbatim copying is only the default
97	
98	This is the decision that most changed shape during design, and it sits in apparent tension with ADR
99	0001, which rejected in-file markers partly because injecting one would mean the installed bytes never
100	equal the source bytes.
101	
102	The resolution is that byte-equality with upstream was never the invariant worth defending. The
103	question that matters is *"does this destination still hold what `harnaas` wrote?"*, and that is
104	answered by comparing the destination against a recorded **installed digest**. A separate **source
105	digest** answers *"has upstream moved?"*. Once those two comparisons are independent, a transformation
106	between source and destination stops being a threat to drift detection, and copying verbatim becomes
107	merely the renderer that happens to apply almost everywhere.
108	
109	Markers remain wrong for the reasons the ADR gives that this does not touch: a comment is not valid
110	syntax in every format, ownership expressed in file content evaporates when someone edits the file,
111	and a marker cannot express "this directory of twelve files is mine". Ownership stays in the lockfile;
112	the bytes are free.
113	
114	The payoff is that `as-skill` — delivering a `command` to a harness with no command surface, as a
115	`SKILL.md` with model invocation disabled — is expressible at all, and that adding a format converter
116	later needs no redesign. The render hook is therefore part of the adapter contract in v1 even though
117	only two renderers exist, because widening an interface after adapters exist is the expensive move.
118	
119	### Refuse rather than produce a silent no-op
120	
121	One principle explains five requirements that otherwise look unrelated and unusually strict:
122	
123	- a `removed` support tier is refused rather than written, because the harness ignores that path;
124	- a skill whose frontmatter `name` disagrees with its inferred id fails resolution, because several
125	  harnesses drop it without a message;
126	- the 1 MB `SKILL.md`, 4 MiB memory file and depth-5 import limits fail the asset, because a file past
127	  them is skipped by the harness;
128	- a declared-but-unimplemented renderer reports `unsupported` and never falls back to identity,
129	  because identity would write a file the harness cannot read;
130	- a `rule` declaring `paths:` is `unsupported` on a harness with no rules directory rather than
131	  emulated as an instruction, because emulation would silently widen it from scoped to always-on.
132	
133	In every case the alternative is a green install and a harness that quietly ignores the file — the
134	single worst outcome for a tool whose whole purpose is telling a team what is actually in effect. The
135	40,000-character assembled-content threshold is deliberately *not* in this list: it is a degradation
136	point, not something the harness enforces, so it warns and never blocks.
137	
138	The name-mismatch check is read-only on purpose. Rewriting the frontmatter to match would fix the
139	symptom, but `harnaas` does not rewrite frontmatter (it would change bytes the author controls, and
140	`paths:` is the case where doing so would change meaning), so the check reports and stops.
141	
142	### Instruction content goes in an `AGENTS.md` block; rules are separate files
143	
144	Recorded in
145	[0003-instruction-content-in-an-agents-md-block.md](../../../docs/adr/0003-instruction-content-in-an-agents-md-block.md).
146	Two details of this change follow from it.
147	
148	Provenance in the block is carried in HTML comments. Claude Code strips HTML comments before the model
149	sees them, so naming each asset and its source costs zero context — which is what makes per-asset
150	attribution affordable in a file that is always in the prompt.
151	
152	`rule` and `instruction` differ on exactly one axis: whether the content survives a fresh clone with
153	nobody having run install. That axis is why instructions are inlined into a committed file while rules
154	are standalone files listed in the ignore block, and why a rule is never referenced from the block or
155	the bridge line. A referenced rule would be an instruction with extra steps.
156	
157	### Installed files are ignored by version control, path by path
158	
159	Installed content is fully reproducible from the manifest plus the lockfile, so committing it
160	duplicates state and turns every upstream bump into a large, meaningless diff. The block in the ignore
161	file lists individual installed paths rather than the directories containing them, which is more
162	verbose and more code, and is required by the shared-target decision: installed and hand-written
163	skills live side by side under the same parent, so `.agents/skills/` as a single entry would untrack
164	somebody's hand-written skill. Precision here is what keeps ADR 0002 from having a nasty second-order
165	cost.
166	
167	### Fetch archives over HTTPS, resolve refs over the Git protocol
168	
169	Three ways to get files out of GitHub were available.
170	
171	Per-file requests through the REST contents API are the obvious approach and the worst: a skill is a
172	directory, so each install needs a listing plus one request per file against a rate limit that is
173	punishing unauthenticated — a CI job installing a handful of skills would exhaust it.
174	
175	Cloning handles private repositories and other forges naturally, but pulls whole history for a few
176	kilobytes of markdown and makes the cache a set of repositories to maintain.
177	
178	Fetching the repository archive for a resolved commit is one request per repository and commit, has no
179	per-file budget, is trivially content-addressable by commit, and reuses archive handling the source
180	CLI already has. Refs are resolved separately over the Git protocol because that path has no API rate
181	limit and goes through the user's existing credential helpers, so a private repository works without
182	`harnaas` inventing an auth story. Resolve names with Git, move bytes over HTTPS.
183	
184	Resolution is split from retrieval for a second reason: ADR
185	[0004-available-updates-are-lint-errors.md](../../../docs/adr/0004-available-updates-are-lint-errors.md)
186	makes an available update a hard failure, which is only coherent if the lockfile retains both what was
187	*asked for* and what it *resolved to*. Recording the requested ref alongside the resolved commit is a
188	requirement of this change that exists entirely to serve that one.
189	
190	### Containment is enforced by the kernel, not by string comparison
191	
192	Both `.harnaas` reads and destination writes go through a handle anchored at the relevant root.
193	Validating a path and then opening it is a time-of-check-to-time-of-use race — a component can become
194	a symbolic link in between — and prefix comparison is notoriously easy to get wrong across platforms.
195	An anchored handle makes escape impossible at the point of use rather than merely improbable at the
196	point of validation, which lets the asset id, the source path and every archive entry name be treated
197	as one class of untrusted input.
198	
199	### Digests cover paths as well as content
200	
201	The whole-source digest is computed over the sorted set of relative paths and their content digests,
202	so renaming a file changes the digest even when no bytes change. Sorting makes the value independent
203	of archive order and filesystem iteration order. Per-file digests recorded alongside it are what let
204	`lint` say *which* file changed rather than only that something did. File modes are normalized rather
205	than hashed, because harness assets are documents and an executable bit carries no meaning worth
206	preserving — and preserving it would make the digest differ across platforms that report modes
207	differently.
208	
209	### Convergence prunes only what it still recognizes
210	
211	Removing an asset from the manifest removes its installed files, so the manifest stays the single
212	description of what a project has, and emptying `assets` is a complete uninstall. Pruning is limited
213	to destinations recorded in the lockfile whose content still matches: if somebody edited an orphan,
214	deleting it would destroy work, so it is kept and reported. A shared destination another recorded
215	harness still claims is likewise kept — attribution is per harness, the file is one file.
216	
217	### The lockfile is committed and decoded leniently
218	
219	An uncommitted lockfile would make ownership a per-machine fact, so a teammate's first install would
220	report every already-installed file as an unmanaged conflict. Committing it also makes `lint` a real
221	CI gate. That forces two further requirements: destinations are stored relative to their scope root
222	with the scope named, so a user-scoped entry does not embed one developer's home directory in a shared
223	file; and decoding ignores unknown fields, because a committed machine-written file is rewritten by
224	every version of the CLI on the team and a newer binary must not brick an older one. Strictness runs
225	the other way for the manifest, which is hand-edited, where an unknown field is a typo worth
226	reporting.
227	
228	### Adapters are decoupled by a test, not by convention
229	
230	An adapter package may import the contract and general utilities, and not the install flow, the
231	lockfile or the command layer. A hand-written AST check parses imports against an allowlist, so
232	widening the boundary is an explicit reviewable edit rather than something that happens during a
233	refactor. The same check asserts every adapter package self-registers, which is the failure mode
234	self-registration is prone to: an adapter that compiles, passes its own tests, and is missing from the
235	registry because nothing imports it.
236	
237	## Risks / Trade-offs
238	
239	- **A shared directory is written for harnesses nobody declared.** Accepted in ADR 0002 and mitigated
240	  here by making the lockfile's harness field attribution rather than ownership, so a destination
241	  survives one harness dropping out while another still claims it.
242	- **Archive fetching downloads a whole repository for a few files.** Fine for asset repositories,
243	  which are documentation-sized, and caching by commit means the cost is paid once. A per-file path
244	  can be added behind the source-kind registry later without touching the install flow.
245	- **Ownership is lost if the lockfile is deleted.** Chosen over embedded markers with eyes open. The
246	  failure is protective — files become unmanaged, not orphaned — and committing the lockfile makes it
247	  rare.
248	- **Pruning deletes files.** The narrowest safe form was chosen: only lockfile-recorded destinations
249	  whose content still matches. A user who edited an orphan keeps their edit.
250	- **Rewriting `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md` and the ignore file touches files users care about.** Mitigated
251	  by writing only inside markers, preserving everything else byte-for-byte, specifying the empty case
252	  so blocks disappear rather than linger, and deleting `CLAUDE.md` only when it holds nothing but the
253	  bridge line. Merge conflicts will land inside the block; that is accepted.
254	- **Refusing rather than warning will annoy people.** A skill whose frontmatter `name` is wrong fails
255	  the install even though the file is perfectly readable, and the remedy is upstream. This is the
256	  deliberate price of never reporting an install that a harness ignores.
257	- **The rendering layer is more machinery than v1 needs.** Two renderers and one adapter do not
258	  require a hook on the contract. It is there because the interface is cheap now and expensive once
259	  adapters exist, and because the two-digest model that makes it safe is needed anyway.
260	- **No authenticity verification.** A compromised upstream serves compromised content and `harnaas`
261	  records its digest faithfully. The lockfile bounds the blast radius: the change is visible as a moved
262	  commit and a changed digest, which is what `lint` reports.
263	- **Manifest and lockfile describe overlapping things and can skew.** Specifying the lockfile here,
264	  with its producer, keeps format and writer together, and skew between the two is itself a finding
265	  `lint` reports.
266	
267	## Open Questions
268	
269	- Whether a future `harnaas adopt` should let a user hand an existing unmanaged file to `harnaas` by
270	  recording it in the lockfile. It would remove the main friction of the unmanaged-conflict default,
271	  but it is additive and not needed to ship.
272	- Whether user-scoped installations belong in the committed lockfile at all, given the destination
273	  exists on one machine. Recorded for now, because `lint` cannot check what it cannot see; revisit if
274	  teams find the shared record noisy.
275	- Which harnesses are known *not* to read the shared skills directory, and therefore need a
276	  per-harness copy. v1 ships one named adapter, so the fallback table is nearly empty and the survey
277	  data behind it will age; it needs a maintenance story before the second adapter lands.

1	// Package source turns a declared source into content harnaas can install.
2	//
3	// The manifest layer parses a source and resolves nothing: `github:acme/assets@v1`
4	// is checked for shape, and whether that repository exists, whether the ref
5	// points anywhere and what is at the path are all questions it deliberately does
6	// not ask. This package answers them, and it is the only place in harnaas that
7	// reaches the network or reads content out of a repository.
8	//
9	// Two things shape it. Every source kind answers the same question — given a
10	// parsed source and a path within it, produce the files and the provenance
11	// needed to record what landed — so the kinds sit behind one contract and a
12	// [Registry] dispatches to them by name. And a resolved source is worthless
13	// unless it can be re-identified later: `lint` has to answer "did somebody edit
14	// this?" and "has upstream moved?" independently, months after the install, from
15	// nothing but what was recorded. That is why a [Resolved] carries a digest per
16	// file and one over the source as a whole, and why the only way to obtain one is
17	// a constructor that computes both.
18	package source
19	
20	import (
21		"context"
22	
23		"github.com/harnaas/harnaas/cmd/harnaas/cli/manifest"
24	)
25	
26	// Kind resolves the sources of one kind for one install run.
27	//
28	// It is created per run rather than registered as a value, because resolution is
29	// not stateless: a repository archive is fetched at most once per repository and
30	// commit per run, and the memory of what has already been fetched belongs to the
31	// run that did it. A kind shared across runs would either leak that memory
32	// between them or need a global cache to hold it.
33	type Kind interface {
34		// Resolve produces the content and provenance for one asset's source.
35		//
36		// It is handed one asset rather than one `sources` entry because the unit
37		// being resolved is the subtree an asset names, and because every diagnostic
38		// raised here has to name the asset the author would go and edit.
39		Resolve(ctx context.Context, req Request) (*Resolved, error)
40	}
41	
42	// NewKind constructs a kind's resolver for one install run. It is what a kind
43	// registers, for the reason [Kind] gives.
44	type NewKind func() Kind
45	
46	// Request is one asset's resolution: the asset being resolved and the `sources`
47	// entry it references.
48	//
49	// The asset travels whole rather than as the two or three fields a kind reads,
50	// because the fields a diagnostic needs are not the fields resolution needs — a
51	// message names the asset's id and its position in the manifest, and narrowing
52	// the request would make every kind's errors worse to keep the struct smaller.
53	type Request struct {
54		// Asset is the manifest entry being resolved, already interpreted: its
55		// reference, type and id are settled before anything is fetched.
56		Asset manifest.Asset
57	
58		// Source is the parsed `sources` entry the asset references. It is the zero
59		// value for the project-local form, which references no entry.
60		Source manifest.Source
61	}
62	
63	// Kind reports which source kind must resolve this request.
64	//
65	// The project-local form declares no `sources` entry and is local by definition
66	// of the manifest grammar, not by anything a caller decides. Answering it here,
67	// once, is what keeps the install flow above and the kinds below from each
68	// restating that rule — and from restating it differently.
69	func (r Request) Kind() manifest.SourceKind {
70		if r.Asset.Ref.Local() {
71			return manifest.SourceKindLocal
72		}
73		return r.Source.Kind
74	}

3	import (
4		"bytes"
5		"crypto/sha256"
6		"encoding/hex"
7		"fmt"
8	)
9	
10	// digestPrefix names the algorithm inside the value itself, so a digest recorded
11	// in the lockfile today stays readable by a binary that hashes differently
12	// tomorrow: it can tell "computed another way" from "the content changed", which
13	// a bare hex string could not.
14	const digestPrefix = "sha256:"
15	
16	// Digest is a content digest, rendered as its algorithm and hexadecimal sum.
17	//
18	// It is a named type because harnaas stores digests beside paths, ids and refs
19	// in the lockfile, and a function taking one should not silently accept any of
20	// those. Comparison is the only operation: harnaas asks whether two digests are
21	// equal and never what they mean.
22	type Digest string
23	
24	// DigestContent returns the digest of one file's bytes.
25	func DigestContent(content []byte) Digest {
26		sum := sha256.Sum256(content)
27		return Digest(digestPrefix + hex.EncodeToString(sum[:]))
28	}
29	
30	// digestFiles returns the digest of a resolved source as a whole.
31	//
32	// Paths participate alongside content, so renaming a file changes the value even
33	// though no byte of it did — a source whose skill moved to a different file is a
34	// different source, and a digest that said otherwise would let `lint` report an
35	// unchanged install for content that no longer lands anywhere.
36	//
37	// File modes are not hashed at all. Harness assets are documents, an executable
38	// bit carries no meaning worth preserving, and hashing one would make the same
39	// content digest differently on platforms that report modes differently — which
40	// would turn a Windows machine and a Linux machine into a permanent disagreement
41	// about whether upstream had moved.
42	//
43	// The files must already be sorted by path, which [NewResolved] guarantees: the
44	// value has to be independent of archive order and of filesystem iteration
45	// order, and sorting at the one place a [Resolved] is built is what makes that a
46	// property of the type rather than a step each kind remembers.
47	func digestFiles(files []File) Digest {
48		var canonical bytes.Buffer
49		for _, file := range files {
50			// The path is length-prefixed because it is untrusted input: an archive
51			// entry may contain any byte, including the separators. Without a frame,
52			// two different sets of files could serialize identically and hash the
53			// same, which is the one failure a content digest may never have.
54			fmt.Fprintf(&canonical, "%d %s %s\n", len(file.Path), file.Path, file.Digest)
55		}
56		return DigestContent(canonical.Bytes())
57	}

11	// Provenance records where a resolved source came from, in the terms the
12	// lockfile stores and `lint` later re-checks.
13	//
14	// The requested ref is kept alongside the commit it resolved to, and the two are
15	// never collapsed. A lockfile holding only the commit could say whether the
16	// installed files still match it, but not whether the tag or branch the manifest
17	// asked for now points somewhere else — which is the whole of update detection.
18	type Provenance struct {
19		// Kind is the source kind that produced the content.
20		Kind manifest.SourceKind
21	
22		// Source is the normalized source, spelled the way the lockfile records it,
23		// so a recorded installation names its origin without the reader consulting
24		// the manifest that was current when it ran.
25		Source string
26	
27		// RequestedRef is the ref the manifest asked for, exactly as written. It is
28		// empty for a kind that has no refs.
29		RequestedRef string
30	
31		// ResolvedCommit is the immutable commit the request resolved to, and the
32		// commit the content was taken from. It is empty for a kind whose content
33		// has no commit.
34		ResolvedCommit string
35	
36		// Mutable reports whether the requested ref can point somewhere else
37		// tomorrow — a branch can, a tag or a commit identifier cannot.
38		//
39		// It is about the ref and not about the content: a local source declares no
40		// ref and so is never mutable, even though the file it names is edited
41		// freely. Whether the bytes changed is a question the digests answer.
42		Mutable bool
43	}
44	
45	// File is one file of a resolved source.
46	type File struct {
47		// Path is the file's location relative to the source's own root, cleaned
48		// and slash-separated on every platform, so a lockfile written on Windows
49		// and one written on Linux record the same install.
50		Path string
51	
52		// Content is the file's bytes, exactly as they arrived. Resolution never
53		// rewrites content — not even a skill's frontmatter, whose `name` it checks
54		// and refuses to correct.
55		Content []byte
56	
57		// Digest is the digest of Content, computed once here so no later phase has
58		// to re-read the file to say which of several files changed.
59		Digest Digest
60	}
61	
62	// Resolved is one asset's source, fetched and verified: every file it consists
63	// of, the digests that re-identify them, and where they came from.
64	//
65	// The content is held in memory rather than left in a directory a caller must
66	// clean up. Harness assets are documents and resolution bounds their total size
67	// before anything is read, so the bytes cost little; what it buys is that
68	// rendering and digesting are pure functions of a value, with no temporary
69	// directory whose lifetime has to outlive the phase that created it.
70	type Resolved struct {
71		// Provenance is where the content came from.
72		Provenance Provenance
73	
74		// Files is every resolved file, sorted by path. Sorted rather than mapped
75		// because this order is what the digest is computed over, what the lockfile
76		// records and what a report lists — three places that must not disagree.
77		Files []File
78	
79		// Digest covers the whole source: every path and every file's digest. It is
80		// what says "upstream moved", independently of the installed digest that
81		// says "somebody edited this".
82		Digest Digest
83	}
84	
85	// errEmptySource reports a resolved source with no files in it.
86	//
87	// It is a distinct error because the condition it prevents is specific: a
88	// retrieval that failed halfway must never be handed on as a source that
89	// legitimately resolved to nothing, which would converge to deleting every file
90	// the asset had installed. Making the constructor refuse it is what turns that
91	// from a rule each kind follows into one none of them can break.
92	var errEmptySource = errors.New("resolved source contains no files")
93	
94	// errEmptyPath reports a file with no path, which would leave the whole-source
95	// digest unable to distinguish it from a file that was not there at all.
96	var errEmptyPath = errors.New("resolved source names a file with an empty path")
97	
98	// NewResolved builds a resolved source from its provenance and its files, given
99	// as the path-to-content mapping extraction produces.
100	//
101	// It is the only way to obtain a [Resolved], so every value of that type has
102	// sorted files, a digest per file and a whole-source digest computed the same
103	// way — a kind cannot produce one whose digest disagrees with its content, and
104	// no later phase has to check that it did.
105	func NewResolved(provenance Provenance, content map[string][]byte) (*Resolved, error) {
106		if len(content) == 0 {
107			return nil, errEmptySource
108		}
109	
110		files := make([]File, 0, len(content))
111		for _, path := range slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(content)) {
112			if path == "" {
113				return nil, errEmptyPath
114			}
115			files = append(files, File{
116				Path:    path,
117				Content: content[path],
118				Digest:  DigestContent(content[path]),
119			})
120		}
121	
122		return &Resolved{Provenance: provenance, Files: files, Digest: digestFiles(files)}, nil
123	}

13	// Registry is the set of source kinds harnaas can resolve, keyed by the name a
14	// manifest writes.
15	//
16	// It exists so that adding a kind is additive: the install flow asks the
17	// registry for a resolver and hands it a request, and contains no branch on
18	// which kind it got. A registry value rather than one package-level map is what
19	// lets a test exercise dispatch — including the failure for a kind nobody
20	// registered — without reaching into the set the binary itself ships.
21	type Registry struct {
22		mu sync.Mutex
23	
24		// kinds holds each kind's constructor rather than a kind, because a kind is
25		// per run. See [Kind].
26		kinds map[manifest.SourceKind]NewKind
27	}
28	
29	// Default is the registry the kinds shipped with this binary register into, and
30	// the one the install flow resolves through. A kind package registers itself
31	// from its own init, so a kind that has been linked in is a kind that works.
32	var Default = &Registry{}
33	
34	// Register adds a kind to [Default].
35	func Register(name manifest.SourceKind, newKind NewKind) {
36		Default.Register(name, newKind)
37	}
38	
39	// Register adds a kind under the name a manifest writes for it.
40	//
41	// A second registration of the same name panics rather than replacing or
42	// ignoring the first. Registration happens during package initialization, before
43	// the process has read anything, so the only way to reach it is a mistake in
44	// harnaas's own wiring — and the two silent outcomes are a binary that resolves
45	// through whichever kind happened to be linked last.
46	func (r *Registry) Register(name manifest.SourceKind, newKind NewKind) {
47		r.mu.Lock()
48		defer r.mu.Unlock()
49	
50		if r.kinds == nil {
51			r.kinds = make(map[manifest.SourceKind]NewKind)
52		}
53		if _, registered := r.kinds[name]; registered {
54			panic(fmt.Sprintf("source: kind %q is registered twice", name))
55		}
56		r.kinds[name] = newKind
57	}
58	
59	// Kinds returns every registered kind name, sorted.
60	//
61	// Sorted rather than in registration order, because registration order is
62	// whatever the import graph happens to produce and this list is rendered into
63	// the error a user reads when their kind is not among them.
64	func (r *Registry) Kinds() []manifest.SourceKind {
65		r.mu.Lock()
66		defer r.mu.Unlock()
67	
68		return r.kindNamesLocked()
69	}
70	
71	// NewResolver constructs one resolver per registered kind and returns the
72	// [Resolver] that dispatches to them, which is the unit of one install run.
73	func (r *Registry) NewResolver() *Resolver {
74		r.mu.Lock()
75		defer r.mu.Unlock()
76	
77		kinds := make(map[manifest.SourceKind]Kind, len(r.kinds))
78		for name, newKind := range r.kinds {
79			kinds[name] = newKind()
80		}
81		return &Resolver{kinds: kinds, registered: r.kindNamesLocked()}
82	}
83	
84	// kindNamesLocked returns the registered names in sorted order. The caller holds
85	// the lock.
86	func (r *Registry) kindNamesLocked() []manifest.SourceKind {
87		names := make([]manifest.SourceKind, 0, len(r.kinds))
88		for name := range r.kinds {
89			names = append(names, name)
90		}
91		slices.Sort(names)
92		return names
93	}
94	
95	// Resolver resolves every source of one install run.
96	//
97	// It holds one live kind per registered name, so the per-run state a kind keeps
98	// — chiefly which repository archives it has already fetched — lives exactly as
99	// long as the run that built it.
100	type Resolver struct {
101		kinds map[manifest.SourceKind]Kind
102	
103		// registered is the sorted name list, captured at construction so the error
104		// for an unsupported kind lists what this run could have resolved rather
105		// than what the registry holds by the time somebody reads the message.
106		registered []manifest.SourceKind
107	}
108	
109	// Resolve resolves one asset's source through the kind that owns it.
110	//
111	// The lookup happens before the kind is asked to do anything, which is what
112	// makes "an unsupported kind reaches no network and writes no file" a property
113	// of the dispatch rather than a rule each kind has to honour on its way in.
114	func (r *Resolver) Resolve(ctx context.Context, req Request) (*Resolved, error) {
115		name := req.Kind()
116	
117		kind, registered := r.kinds[name]
118		if !registered {
119			return nil, &UnsupportedKindError{Kind: name, Registered: slices.Clone(r.registered)}
120		}
121	
122		return kind.Resolve(ctx, req)
123	}
124	
125	// UnsupportedKindError reports a source kind no registered kind can resolve.
126	//
127	// The manifest layer rejects a kind its grammar does not know, so reaching this
128	// means a kind harnaas parses but this binary cannot fetch — an older binary
129	// meeting a manifest written for a newer one. That is why the remedy is an
130	// upgrade rather than an edit, and why the error is a type: the install flow
131	// attributes it to the asset that carried the source.
132	type UnsupportedKindError struct {
133		// Kind is the unresolvable kind, exactly as the manifest wrote it.
134		Kind manifest.SourceKind
135	
136		// Registered is every kind this binary can resolve, sorted.
137		Registered []manifest.SourceKind
138	}
139	
140	// Error states the problem and then the fix, as every user-facing diagnostic
141	// does.
142	func (e *UnsupportedKindError) Error() string {
143		names := make([]string, 0, len(e.Registered))
144		for _, name := range e.Registered {
145			names = append(names, string(name))
146		}
147	
148		return fmt.Sprintf(
149			"this harnaas cannot resolve sources of kind %q\n\n"+
150				"Upgrade harnaas, or declare a source of a kind it installs: %s.",
151			e.Kind, strings.Join(names, ", "),
152		)
153	}

### There is one fetcher, and a URL is redacted by the type that prints it

`source.Fetcher` is the only way harnaas makes an HTTP request, and it holds every transport rule at
once: https only, never a destination on this machine, a bounded redirect chain, a total timeout and
a size ceiling. The rules live beside the source contract rather than inside the one kind that
fetches today, because a forge added later must not be able to make a request that skips them — and
the only structural way to guarantee that is for there to be no exported way to build a second
fetcher. The destination rule runs again on **every redirect hop**: Go's default policy follows ten
redirects across schemes and hosts and only the URL harnaas built was ever checked, so an https entry
point could otherwise deliver the archive over plaintext from anywhere. Loopback is refused because
content already on this machine is what a `local` source under `.harnaas` is for, so a hop aimed here
is either a misconfiguration or a redirect at a service that never expected an outside request. The
one exemption is unexported and exists so the suite can serve a body at all.

The body is read one byte past the ceiling and buffered whole. A bare `io.LimitReader` stops at the
limit and reports success, so an oversized archive would arrive truncated, extract, and have its
digest recorded as though it were the real content — the failure a content digest may never have.
Returning bytes rather than a stream is what makes "no partial body reaches a caller" structural.

Every URL harnaas prints, logs or writes goes through `source.RedactURL`, which drops userinfo **and
the query string**: an archive download redirects to a signed URL whose `token=` grants the bearer
the access the request had, so a redaction that removed only userinfo would have looked right and
leaked the credential harnaas actually meets. Each transport error holds the URL raw and redacts
where its message is built, so redaction is a property of the type rather than a step every caller
constructing one has to remember — and a cause is unwrapped out of its `url.Error` before it is
